1.title: The Accent I Keep Losing
paragraphs: For the first few months after I moved to Edinburgh, I was forever being asked where I was from. It was a reasonable question, and I had been answering it, in one form or another, since I was nineteen. What I had not anticipated was that the question would gradually change shape. By my third winter, people had stopped asking where I was from and had started asking where I had been. My accent, it seemed, had been quietly packing its bags.

Linguists have a rather unromantic name for this: accommodation. When we talk to others, we tend to adjust our speech towards theirs, usually without noticing. Over years, those small, temporary adjustments can harden into something more permanent. The vowels flatten or stretch; the rhythm of a sentence begins to rise where it once fell. None of this is unusual. What is unusual, I think, is how personally we take it.

I say this because I have been taking it very personally indeed. On a recent visit home to Valparaíso, an aunt I had not seen for a decade listened to me for about thirty seconds before announcing, with the bluntness reserved for close family, that I was sounding like a foreigner. She was not being unkind; she was, if anything, being affectionate. But I found myself replaying the remark for days afterwards, as if she had caught me out in a lie.

The lie, if that is what it was, lay in the assumption that the way I speak is a fixed fact about me, like my height or the shape of my hands. Psychologists who study identity have long argued otherwise. Our sense of self, they suggest, is less a possession than a performance, something we are continually doing rather than something we simply have. On this view, an accent is not a birthmark but a costume we have been wearing for so long that we have forgotten it can come off.

The trouble with that argument is that it sounds liberating on paper and feels like loss in practice. I have been weighing it up for months now, and I am still not sure whether I am growing or dissolving. When I catch myself saying 'wee' instead of 'small', I feel a flicker of pride at having belonged somewhere new, followed almost immediately by a pang of guilt, as though I have been unfaithful to the people who taught me to talk.

A researcher I spoke to in Glasgow, who has been recording migrants' speech for nearly twenty years, was gently amused by my anxiety. 'People imagine there's a single original voice that's being eroded,' she told me. 'But nobody has only one voice. You've always been speaking differently to your grandmother and to your boss. Migration just makes the range more audible.' She pointed out that many of the people she had interviewed had been switching between accents several times a day, often within a single conversation, and that most of them regarded this not as a betrayal but as a skill.

I wanted to ask her whether she had ever felt the same unease herself, but I hesitated, and the moment passed. Later, I emailed to say I was wondering if she might be willing to talk about her own experience. Her reply was brief and characteristically generous: she had been a Liverpudlian in London, a Londoner in Toronto and a 'posh English woman' in Glasgow, and she had long since given up deciding which of them was the real one.

There is something consoling in that. The demand that we be one thing, consistently and forever, is a fairly recent and fairly peculiar expectation. For most of human history, people who moved, traded or married across borders would have had to sound different in different places simply to be understood. The idea that a shift in pronunciation amounts to a shift in loyalty would, I suspect, have puzzled them.

None of which means the unease will disappear. Belonging, after all, is not only something we feel; it is something other people grant or withhold. My aunt's remark stung precisely because it seemed to suggest that home had quietly revoked my membership. Yet the next morning, she was teasing me about it over breakfast, and by the end of the week she had stopped mentioning it altogether. I had not changed back. She had simply been getting used to the newer version of me, as families eventually do.

So I have decided, provisionally, to stop worrying about which accent is authentic. I am being, I suppose, a little more forgiving of myself. The voice I have now is the record of everywhere I have lived and everyone I have listened to. It is not the voice I started with. But then, I am not the person I started as, and I would be rather disappointed if I were.

1.title: Home Is a Verb
paragraphs: For most of my childhood, the question 'Where's home?' was the conversational equivalent of a trapdoor. Asked casually at a party or a school gate, it seemed to expect a single word in reply: a city, a country, a dot on a map. I had several dots and no confidence about which one counted. My father's job had taken us from Lagos to Rotterdam, from Rotterdam to Kuala Lumpur and finally to a town on the south coast of England that none of us had heard of until the removal van pulled up outside. By the time I was twelve, I had been the new girl five times.

Sociologists have a label for children like me: 'third culture kids', people raised in a culture other than that of their parents for a significant part of their development. The label was coined in the 1950s, and it has been doing a great deal of work ever since, appearing in university admissions essays, corporate relocation brochures and, more recently, in a cottage industry of memoirs. I resisted it for years. It sounded less like a description than a diagnosis, as though rootlessness were a condition one might eventually be cured of.

What changed my mind was not a book but a conversation with my grandmother, who had never left the region where she was born. I had gone to stay with her one summer when I was in my twenties, and I was complaining, at some length, that I did not really belong anywhere. She let me finish, then asked what I meant by 'belong'. I said something about feeling at ease, being understood, not having to explain myself. She considered this for a moment and said: 'Then you're asking for something nobody has. I've lived in this village for eighty years, and I'm still explaining myself every day.'

I have been thinking about that remark, on and off, for almost two decades. It took me a long time to see what she was doing. She was not dismissing my unease; she was relocating it. I had assumed that people with a single, uncomplicated origin possessed something I lacked, a kind of passive membership that required no effort. She was telling me that belonging, even for those who appear to have it by birthright, is not a state but an activity. It has to be renewed, negotiated, occasionally defended. It is, to borrow a phrase I have since come across in several places, a verb rather than a noun.

This idea has its critics, and they are not wrong to be wary. To describe belonging as something we do can sound uncomfortably like blaming people who are excluded for not trying hard enough. A refugee who has been waiting years for papers is not failing to 'do' belonging; she is being prevented from it. Any honest account has to admit that some doors are locked from the inside, by laws, by prejudice, by the quiet refusal of neighbours to say good morning.

Still, within those limits, I have found the verb more useful than the noun. If home is a place, then I have lost several and will never recover them; the flat in Rotterdam has since been demolished, and the school in Kuala Lumpur has moved to another district. If home is something I make, then I have been making it all along, in the habits I carry from one kitchen to the next, in the songs I sing without realising I know the words, in the friends who have known me in three languages.

I notice, too, that I have stopped apologising for the complicated answer. When someone asks where I am from these days, I tend to ask them how long they have got. Most laugh; a few look genuinely curious; one or two, I suspect, are hoping for the short version and are disappointed. That is fine. The short version was never true, and I have spent too long pretending that it might be.

My own children, who were both born in the town where we now live, are growing up with a single dot on the map. I used to imagine that this would spare them the trapdoor. I am less sure now. My daughter, who is fourteen, has lately been insisting that she does not feel at home in the town at all, that she is only waiting to leave. I was tempted to tell her how lucky she was. Instead, I found myself repeating what her great-grandmother told me. Belonging is not something you are given and then keep. It is something you keep doing, or it slowly stops being yours.
She rolled her eyes, as fourteen-year-olds do. But the next evening, I noticed, she had invited a classmate round for dinner.

2.title: The Rumour That Outran Its Correction
paragraphs: It was on a Tuesday afternoon in March that the rumour first appeared, and by Thursday it had reached, by one estimate, a third of the town. Someone had posted a photograph of a water treatment plant, its outflow stained an alarming shade of orange, along with the claim that the local council had known about contamination for months and said nothing. The photograph was real. The claim was not. The orange colour, as the council explained within hours, came from a harmless mineral deposit disturbed during routine maintenance, and independent tests confirmed that the water was safe to drink.

What happened next is the part that interests researchers. Not only did the correction fail to stop the rumour; in some neighbourhoods, sales of bottled water actually rose after it was published. Six weeks later, a survey found that almost half of those who had seen both the original post and the council's statement still believed the water had been unsafe. Many of them could accurately recall the correction. They simply did not let it change their minds.

Psychologists call this the continued influence effect, and it is far from new. In laboratory studies going back decades, participants who are told a false detail about an event, and later told explicitly that the detail was wrong, continue to rely on it when asked to explain what happened. What seems to matter is not whether people remember the retraction but whether the retraction leaves a gap. If a story makes sense with the false detail and stops making sense without it, the mind will cling to the detail rather than tolerate an unexplained hole.

This is why bare denials so often backfire. 'The water is not contaminated' asks the listener to discard an explanation without offering a replacement. Worse, it repeats the very words, water and contaminated, that formed the original claim, and repetition, as advertisers have always understood, breeds familiarity. Rarely does a correction travel as far or as fast as the falsehood it targets, and seldom does it arrive carrying the same emotional charge. A photograph of orange water is vivid; a paragraph about mineral deposits is not.

So what does work? The evidence, while far from conclusive, points in a few consistent directions. The first is that it is the alternative explanation, rather than the denial itself, that does most of the work. Corrections that tell people what actually happened, and why the misleading impression arose, tend to be more effective than those that merely insist the original claim is false. In the case of the water plant, it was only when the council published a short video of an engineer scraping the orange sediment from a pipe that the bottled-water sales began to fall.

The second is timing. Researchers have experimented with what they call prebunking, a kind of inoculation in which people are warned in advance about the techniques used to mislead them. Participants shown a brief explanation of, say, how emotionally loaded images are used to bypass scepticism become noticeably better at resisting such images later. Well established this approach is not, and its long-term effects remain uncertain. But the logic is appealing: it is easier to keep a false belief out than to dig it up once it has taken root.

The third, and perhaps the most uncomfortable, concerns the messenger. People are far more likely to accept a correction from someone they regard as being on their side. In the town in question, the council was already unpopular, having closed a library and raised parking charges the previous year. What persuaded many sceptics, according to the local newspaper, was not the official statement but a post from a well-known retired nurse, who filmed herself filling a glass from her kitchen tap and drinking it. Little did she expect that her thirty-second clip would be watched more times than every council announcement that year combined.

None of this should be taken to mean that facts are powerless. On the contrary, the research suggests that most people do update their beliefs when presented with clear, credible information; they simply do so more slowly, and less completely, than we might wish. The problem lies less in human irrationality than in the mismatch between how quickly a vivid story spreads and how slowly a careful correction follows.

Perhaps the most striking lesson of the orange water episode is how little the original poster seems to have intended. Interviewed months later, he said he had been genuinely worried and had shared the image to warn his neighbours. Only afterwards did he realise how many people had taken his speculation as fact. 'What I should have written,' he said, 'was a question, not an answer.' It is a distinction worth remembering, and one that rather more of us might bear in mind before pressing share.

2.title: In Defence of Rhetoric
paragraphs: Rhetoric has a reputation problem. Say that a politician's speech was 'mere rhetoric' and everyone knows what you mean: it was empty, manipulative, more interested in sounding good than in being true. The word has become a polite synonym for spin. Yet for most of Western intellectual history, rhetoric was regarded not as a vice but as a discipline, one of the three foundations of education alongside grammar and logic. What I want to argue here is that we abandoned that view at our cost, and that the remedy for bad persuasion is not less rhetoric but more of it, better taught and more widely understood.

Consider first what rhetoric actually is. Stripped of its connotations, it is simply the study of how language moves people: how arguments are arranged, how examples are chosen, how a sentence can be shaped so that its most important word lands at the moment of greatest attention. None of this is inherently deceptive. A doctor explaining a diagnosis to a frightened patient uses rhetoric. So does a teacher who chooses a story rather than a statistic to make a point stick. What distinguishes honest persuasion from manipulation is not the presence of technique but the purpose to which it is put.

Critics will object that this is naive. Technique, they will say, is morally neutral in theory but rarely in practice, and those most skilled in it tend to be those with most to gain. There is something in this. Seldom has the gap between eloquence and integrity been more conspicuous than in the career of the charismatic demagogue, and anyone who has watched a crowd being worked up by a skilled speaker will understand the instinct to distrust the whole enterprise. But the conclusion does not follow. That a skill can be abused is an argument for spreading it, not for surrendering it to those who will abuse it.

Here the historical record is instructive. In ancient Athens, the teaching of rhetoric was controversial precisely because it was democratising: it gave citizens without wealth or connections the tools to argue their case in the assembly and the courts. The philosophers who denounced the professional teachers of rhetoric did so partly on principle and partly, one suspects, because they disliked seeing the advantages of a privileged education handed out for a fee. The pattern recurs. Those who can already persuade are often the first to insist that persuasion is beneath us.

What we lose when rhetoric disappears from the curriculum is not the practice of persuasion, which continues regardless, but the capacity to recognise it. A student who has never been taught how an argument can be framed is at the mercy of whoever frames it first. She may sense that a speech is manipulative without being able to say why, and an objection one cannot articulate is easily dismissed. By contrast, a listener who can identify a false dilemma, a loaded term or an appeal to fear has a defence that no fact-checking website can provide, because it travels with her into every conversation.

Nor should we overlook the positive case. Democratic life depends on people being able to make their views heard by those who do not already share them. That is a rhetorical task. It requires knowing one's audience, anticipating objections, conceding what must be conceded and pressing what can be pressed. A movement that cannot do these things will lose to one that can, however strong its arguments on paper. It is no accident that the most effective reformers of the last two centuries were, almost without exception, formidable rhetoricians.

I am not suggesting that teaching rhetoric would cure our public discourse overnight. Some people will always prefer a comforting falsehood to an uncomfortable truth, and no amount of training will change that. Nor am I claiming that every persuasive technique is equally acceptable; there is a real moral difference between an appeal to shared values and an appeal to tribal resentment. Precisely because the difference matters, though, we need citizens equipped to notice it.

So when I hear a speech dismissed as 'mere rhetoric', I am inclined to ask a different question. Not whether the speaker was using rhetoric, since all speakers are, but whether it was used well or badly, honestly or otherwise, and whether the audience had the means to tell. Only when we can answer that question will we be in a position to judge. Until then, the phrase 'mere rhetoric' tells us more about the listener's lack of training than about the speaker's lack of substance.

3.title: The Witness Who Was Certain
paragraphs: The woman in the witness box was not lying. Of that, everyone in the courtroom seemed sure, and they were right. She had been at the bus stop on the evening in question; she had seen a man run from the newsagent's with a bag under his arm; she had looked straight at his face under the street light for perhaps two seconds. When she was asked whether the man was in court, she pointed at the defendant without hesitation. 'I'll never forget that face,' she said. It was the most persuasive moment of the trial, and it was almost certainly mistaken.

We now know this because, three years later, another man confessed to the robbery and was able to describe details that only the culprit could have known. The defendant, who had spent those three years in prison, was released. The witness, interviewed afterwards, was distraught. She had not invented anything. She had simply remembered, with complete sincerity, something that had never quite happened in the way she recalled it.

Cases like this have transformed the way psychologists think about memory. For much of the twentieth century, the popular model was something like a video recording: events were captured, stored and later played back, perhaps with some loss of quality over time. That model, we can now say with some confidence, must be wrong. Memory is not retrieved so much as rebuilt. Each time we recall an event, we reconstruct it from fragments, filling the gaps with expectation, inference and whatever information has reached us since.

Consider what the witness would have experienced that evening. The light will have been poor; the man was moving; she was frightened. Under such conditions, the brain captures surprisingly little detail about a stranger's face. What it captures instead is a general impression, an outline into which later information can easily be poured. When, a week later, police showed her a set of photographs, the outline may well have been filled in by the face she saw there. By the time she reached the courtroom, she could not have distinguished between what she had seen at the bus stop and what she had seen in the police station. Nor would she have had any reason to try.

The most unsettling finding of this research is that confidence and accuracy are only loosely connected. A witness who has rehearsed a memory several times, been encouraged by an officer ('Good, that's our suspect') and seen the defendant's face in newspapers will typically become more certain, not less, as the trial approaches. Juries, understandably, find certainty persuasive. A witness who says 'I think it might have been him' sounds weaker than one who says 'It was definitely him', even though the hesitant witness may be the more reliable of the two.

None of this means that eyewitnesses are worthless. Under the right conditions, initial identifications made quickly and with appropriate caution can be reasonably accurate. The problem lies in the conditions. Many of the safeguards now recommended by researchers are strikingly simple: the officer conducting an identification should not know which person in the line-up is the suspect, so that she cannot unconsciously signal it; the witness should be told that the culprit might not be present at all; and her level of confidence should be recorded at once, in her own words, before anything has had the chance to inflate it.

It is tempting to read stories like this as a warning about other people's memories. That would be a mistake. Most of us will have had the experience of recounting an anecdote for years, only to be told by a sibling that we have got it all wrong: it was not you who fell in the river but your cousin; it was not summer but late autumn. Our first reaction will usually be disbelief. Surely we cannot have invented a memory so vivid? But vividness, it turns out, is no guarantee. Some of our most cherished recollections may be composites, assembled over decades from photographs, family stories and things we were told we did.

The witness in the robbery case later said that she wished someone had warned her. 'I needn't have been so sure,' she said, 'but nobody told me that being sure wasn't the same as being right.' It is hard to think of a more useful sentence to put before a jury, or before ourselves. Our memories are not liars. They are storytellers, and like all storytellers they will tend to improve the tale with every telling.

3.title: The Blue Door
paragraphs: The house, when Tomás finally found it, had a green door. He stood on the opposite pavement for some time, holding the paper bag of pastries he had bought as a kind of offering, and tried to make the door turn blue. It would not. It was green, a deep bottle green, and the paint around the letterbox was flaking in a way that suggested it had been green for years.

He must have got the street wrong. That was the obvious explanation, and he clung to it for nearly a minute. But the street was right. There was the lamppost with the dent in it, at about the height a small boy's bicycle handlebar would reach; there was the low wall where his grandmother would sit in the evenings, shelling peas into a bowl and passing comment on everyone who walked by. The wall was shorter than he remembered, which he had expected. Walls always were. The door, he had not expected.

He had told the story of the blue door so often that it had become a sort of signature. At dinner parties, when people swapped memories of childhood, he would describe it: the colour of a swimming pool, he would say, the colour of a summer sky over the harbour, so bright that the postman used to joke he needed sunglasses to deliver the letters. He would describe his grandmother repainting it every spring, standing on a kitchen chair, and the smell of the paint mingling with the smell of bread from the bakery on the corner. People liked the story. He had liked telling it.
The bakery, he now noticed, was a mobile phone shop.

A woman came out of the house next door, glanced at him, and then glanced again, with the particular wariness reserved for men who stand too long on pavements. He crossed the road and, because he could think of nothing else to do, explained. He had lived here as a boy, he said, with his grandmother, forty years ago. He had come back for the first time. He was sorry to be staring. It was only that he remembered the door as blue.

'Blue?' She considered the door as if it might be at fault. 'I've been here since nineteen eighty-six. It's always been green, as far as I know. The old lady before the current owners, she'd have it repainted every few years, but always the same colour. She was very particular.' She paused. 'Your grandmother, would that have been? Señora Ibáñez?'

He nodded. It was absurd how much he wanted the woman to say that she remembered a blue door after all, that there had been a brief, glorious blue period in the early eighties that everyone had since forgotten. She did not say this. Instead she said that his grandmother had been a formidable woman who would tell you exactly what she thought of your haircut, and that the street had been quieter without her. Then, perhaps sensing that he needed something, she added: 'She'll have told everyone about you, you know. The grandson in the north. We all knew your name.'

Afterwards, sitting on the low wall with the pastries untouched beside him, he tried to work out where the blue had come from. He could not have made it up out of nothing; memories did not work like that, did they? Perhaps there had been a blue door somewhere else: a neighbour's, a friend's, a door in a book he had loved. Perhaps it had been the sky reflected in the glass panel that he now saw, looking more carefully, was set into the top of the green door. Perhaps, at some dinner party long ago, he had simply said blue because it sounded better than green, and the lie had been repeated until it hardened into truth.

He found, to his surprise, that he did not much mind which it was. He needn't have come all this way to check, he supposed; he could have gone on telling the story, and nobody would ever have known. But he had not come to check the door. He had come, he realised, to see whether anything of her was still here. And something was: in the wall, in the dented lamppost, in a neighbour who still remembered her opinions about haircuts.

When he finally stood up to leave, he left the pastries on the wall. Someone would find them. His grandmother, he thought, would have approved; she had never been able to bear waste. And as he walked back towards the station, he caught himself rehearsing a new version of the story, one in which the door was green, and the colour mattered less than he had always believed.

4.title: The Uneasy Arithmetic of Merit
paragraphs: Few ideas enjoy such broad approval as meritocracy. Ask politicians on the left and the right what kind of society they want, and most will describe some version of it: a system in which positions are allocated on the basis of talent and effort rather than birth or connections. The appeal is obvious. A meritocracy promises fairness to those at the bottom and legitimacy to those at the top. Its critics, however, have become increasingly vocal, and their objections deserve closer attention than they usually receive.

The first objection concerns the measurement of merit itself. Talent and effort are not directly observable; what institutions observe instead are proxies such as examination results, degrees from prestigious universities and records of previous employment. These proxies are far from neutral. A child growing up in a household filled with books, supported by private tuition and spared the need to earn money during her studies, will arrive at the examination hall with advantages unrelated to any innate ability. The resulting scores, presented as objective evidence of merit, are in part a measurement of accumulated privilege.

Defenders of meritocracy acknowledge this but argue that the solution lies in the improvement of measurement rather than its abandonment. Widening access to good schools, introducing contextual admissions that take an applicant's background into account, and the removal of unpaid internships as a route into certain professions are all reforms aimed at bringing the proxies closer to what they are meant to capture. There is substantial evidence that such measures, carefully implemented, can make a meaningful difference.

The second objection is subtler and, for many, more troubling. It concerns not the accuracy of the system but its psychological effects on winners and losers alike. In a society that believes its rewards are distributed according to merit, success becomes a moral verdict as well as an economic outcome. Those who prosper are encouraged to regard their position as deserved, and those who struggle are left with the implication that their failure is, at some level, their own fault. Researchers studying attitudes to inequality have found that belief in meritocracy is associated with greater tolerance of large income gaps and, in some studies, with reduced sympathy for people living in poverty.

The irony here is considerable. The original coinage of the word 'meritocracy', in a satirical novel published in 1958, was intended as a warning. The book imagined a future Britain in which intelligence testing had replaced inherited privilege, and in which the resulting elite, convinced of its own superiority, had become more arrogant and less compassionate than the aristocracy it displaced. The author lived to see the word adopted as a slogan by the very politicians whose assumptions he had set out to mock, and he did not hesitate to say so.

A third line of criticism points to the role of luck. Even setting aside inherited advantages, outcomes in competitive fields are shaped by chance to a degree that participants rarely acknowledge. Being born in a particular month can affect a child's chances of being selected for sports teams; graduating during a recession can depress earnings for a decade; a single encounter with the right mentor can redirect a career. The successful, studies suggest, consistently underestimate the contribution of such factors, preferring to remember the hours of effort rather than the fortunate timing.

None of this amounts to an argument for abandoning merit as a principle. A surgeon should be selected for her competence, not her surname, and few would wish to return to a world of hereditary office. What the critics are proposing is rather a shift in emphasis: from the celebration of individual achievement towards the recognition of the conditions that make achievement possible. This might involve greater investment in the early years, when gaps in opportunity first open up, or a renewed respect for forms of work that do not require academic credentials but are nonetheless essential to the functioning of society.

There is also a case for a little more humility at the top. The executive who stops to consider how much of her success depended on circumstances beyond her control is not thereby diminished. If anything, the acknowledgement of good fortune tends to be accompanied by a greater willingness to share its benefits. The question, perhaps, is not whether merit should matter, but whether we can learn to reward it without mistaking our rewards for proof of our virtue.

Meritocracy, in the end, may be best understood as an aspiration rather than a description. As an aspiration, it remains powerful and worth pursuing. As a description of how any existing society actually works, it is, at best, an incomplete account, and at worst a comforting story told by the fortunate about themselves.

4.title: A Curriculum Vitae of Failures
paragraphs: A few years ago, a university lecturer did something that, by the standards of academic life, bordered on the reckless. Alongside his conventional curriculum vitae, with its list of degrees, publications and prizes, he published a second document listing everything he had applied for and not got: the fellowships declined, the journals that had rejected his papers, the jobs that had gone to someone else. The second list was considerably longer than the first. It was also, by a wide margin, the more widely read.

I remember reading it at the time and feeling a peculiar mixture of relief and unease. Relief, because it confirmed what anyone who has tried to build a career in a competitive field suspects: that the polished record of achievement presented on a CV is a highly selective account, edited to remove the setbacks that made the successes possible. Unease, because I could not quite decide whether the exercise was an act of honesty or a more sophisticated form of self-promotion. Only someone whose position was secure, after all, could afford to advertise his failures.

That objection has some force. A 'failure CV' published by a tenured professor is not the same thing as one published by a graduate struggling to find her first post. For the professor, the list of rejections serves as a charming footnote to a story whose ending is already known. For the graduate, it might be read by a prospective employer as evidence of unsuitability. The candour that one person can afford is a risk that another cannot.

And yet I have come to think that the exercise matters, not for what it reveals about any individual but for what it reveals about the system. Consider the arithmetic. In many fields, the success rate for applications to major funding bodies hovers somewhere between ten and twenty per cent. A researcher submitting ten proposals can therefore expect to have eight or nine of them turned down, even if every one is of high quality. Rejection, under such conditions, is not a sign of failure but a structural feature of the process. Treating it as a personal verdict is both inaccurate and corrosive.

The problem is that we rarely see the arithmetic. What we see are the outcomes: the colleague who has just won the grant, the former classmate whose start-up has been acquired, the friend whose novel is in the shop window. Each of these achievements arrives detached from the dozens of attempts that preceded it, and our own failures, by contrast, are experienced in full, one painful email at a time. It is a comparison rigged against us, and it is hardly surprising that so many people in competitive professions report feeling like impostors.

I tried keeping a failure CV of my own for a while, partly as an experiment and partly as a form of therapy. The results were instructive. Within a year, the document contained eleven rejections, three projects abandoned for lack of funding, and one memorable occasion on which I was shortlisted for a post and then forgot to attend the interview because I had written down the wrong date. Looking back over the list, I was struck less by its length than by how few of the entries I still regretted. Most had led, often by circuitous routes, to something else: a different collaboration, a better idea, a job I had not known existed.

This is not to romanticise failure, which is often simply painful and occasionally ruinous. Some setbacks do not lead anywhere useful, and the cheerful insistence that every rejection is a hidden opportunity can be its own kind of tyranny. I regret to say that I have encountered this attitude most often among people who have never experienced a serious failure themselves. But there is a difference between pretending that failure is good and admitting that it is normal. The second is merely accurate; the first is a sales pitch.

What would change if more of us were willing to make that admission? Perhaps not very much at first. Institutions are slow to alter the habits by which they evaluate people, and a CV that lists rejections will continue to be read, in many quarters, with suspicion. But culture is shaped by small acts of disclosure as much as by policy. A senior colleague who mentions, in passing, that her first three applications were unsuccessful gives junior staff a permission that no mentoring scheme can provide.

I meant to stop the experiment after a year. I have gone on keeping the list, somewhat to my own surprise, and I now consult it more often than I consult my conventional CV. It is a less flattering document, certainly. It is also a more truthful one, and on difficult days it reminds me of something the polished version conceals: that the people whose careers I envy have almost certainly failed more often than I have, and simply went on applying.

5.title: The Algorithm Will See You Now
paragraphs: The radiologist I spent a morning with in a large teaching hospital is, by her own admission, slightly embarrassed by how much she has come to rely on her new colleague. The colleague does not drink coffee, never asks for leave and is reported to have examined more chest X-rays in its first year than she will see in her entire career. It is a piece of software, and it is one of a growing number of artificial intelligence systems that are said to be transforming the way diseases are detected.

The claims made for such systems are, on the face of it, remarkable. Algorithms trained on millions of images are believed to be capable of spotting early signs of lung cancer, diabetic eye disease and certain skin conditions with an accuracy that matches, and in some studies exceeds, that of experienced specialists. In regions where specialists are scarce, the technology is expected to allow patients to have their scans assessed within hours rather than weeks. It is not difficult to see why health ministries are enthusiastic.

It would appear, however, that the reality is somewhat more complicated than the headlines suggest. Much of the evidence for these systems comes from retrospective studies, in which an algorithm is tested on a collection of images whose diagnoses are already known. Such studies are useful, but they are generally considered to be a poor guide to performance in the messy conditions of a working hospital, where scanners vary, patients move and images are taken by staff of differing experience. Several systems that performed impressively in the laboratory are understood to have proved disappointing once deployed.

There is also the question of what the algorithms have actually learned. In one widely discussed case, a system designed to detect a particular lung condition was found to have been relying in part on the type of scanner used, since patients who were seriously ill tended to be scanned with portable machines at their bedside. The software had not learned to recognise the disease so much as to recognise the circumstances in which the disease was likely to be found. Errors of this kind are thought to be more common than published results might indicate, precisely because they are difficult to detect without careful investigation.

Concerns about bias are, arguably, more serious still. An algorithm can only be as representative as the data on which it was trained. If those data were collected predominantly from one population, the system may perform less well for patients who differ from that population in skin tone, age or genetic background. Developers are now being urged to have their training data audited for such imbalances before seeking approval, although it remains unclear how consistently this is done.

None of these difficulties, it should be stressed, is necessarily insurmountable, and few of the clinicians I spoke to wished to see the technology abandoned. What most of them did wish for was a more measured conversation about its place. The radiologist put it this way: the software is very good at noticing things, but it is not responsible for what happens next. When it flags a shadow on a scan, it is she who must decide whether to have the patient recalled, whether to order further tests, how to explain the uncertainty to a frightened family. Those decisions are not merely technical. They involve judgement, communication and accountability, and it is by no means clear that these can be delegated to a machine.

The question of accountability is likely to become pressing. If an algorithm fails to detect a tumour that a human would have spotted, who is to blame: the hospital that bought the system, the company that built it, or the doctor who trusted it? At present, the answer would seem to be the doctor, since most systems are approved only as aids to human decision-making. Yet as the software becomes more accurate, the temptation to defer to it will presumably grow, and the line between assistance and replacement may become increasingly difficult to draw.

Some ethicists have suggested that patients should be told whenever an algorithm has been involved in their diagnosis, and given the opportunity to have their results reviewed by a human specialist if they so wish. Others regard this as impractical, pointing out that patients are not normally informed about the many other tools, from blood analysers to dosage calculators, that shape their care. The disagreement reflects a deeper uncertainty about whether AI is merely another instrument, or something qualitatively different.

What seems reasonably certain is that the technology will not go away. The radiologist, for her part, has made her peace with it. She has had the software configured so that it shows her its suggestions only after she has formed her own opinion, a small precaution she describes as 'keeping my eye in'. It is, perhaps, a model worth considering more widely: not a choice between human and machine, but an arrangement in which each is used to check the other.

5.title: What Your Spit Says About Your Cousins
paragraphs: It has never been easier to have your genome read. For the price of a pair of trainers, a company will post you a small plastic tube; you spit into it, send it back, and a few weeks later receive an account of your ancestry, your likely tolerance for caffeine and, if you pay a little more, your predisposition to certain diseases. Millions of people have done so, and the practice is widely regarded as a harmless diversion, somewhere between a horoscope and a family tree. I want to suggest that this view is, at the very least, incomplete.

The difficulty begins with a fact about genetics that is easily overlooked. Your DNA is not only yours. You share roughly half of it with each parent and each sibling, a quarter with each grandparent, and smaller but still identifiable portions with cousins you may never have met. When you have your sample analysed, you are therefore disclosing information about dozens of other people, none of whom has been asked for consent. The decision is presented as a personal one, but its consequences are, by their nature, collective.

This might seem an abstract concern, were it not for the uses to which genetic databases have already been put. In several countries, investigators are known to have identified suspects in long-unsolved crimes by uploading DNA from a crime scene to genealogy websites and searching for partial matches among the suspect's relatives. The relatives themselves had not been accused of anything; they had simply submitted samples out of curiosity about their heritage. Whatever one thinks of the outcome in particular cases, it is difficult to argue that those who took part did so on the understanding that their data might be used in this way.

Defenders of the industry point out, reasonably enough, that most companies now ask customers whether they wish their data to be available for law enforcement searches, and that many customers say yes. They also note that genetic information has contributed to important medical research, and that participants are often motivated by a genuine wish to help. Both points have merit. Yet consent obtained through a box ticked at the end of a lengthy online form is, it could be argued, a rather thin form of agreement, particularly when the implications extend to people who never saw the form at all.

There are, moreover, questions about permanence. A password that has been stolen can be changed; a genome cannot. Data that is held securely today may be sold, merged or leaked tomorrow, should the company that holds it be acquired, go bankrupt or suffer a breach. Several firms in the sector are reported to have been in financial difficulty in recent years, and it is not always clear what becomes of their databases when they change hands. Customers who had their samples processed a decade ago may have no idea where their information currently resides.

It would be wrong to suggest that the risks are purely hypothetical, but equally wrong to exaggerate them. Most people who take a genetic test will experience nothing worse than a mildly surprising revelation about their great-grandparents. Some will learn things they would have preferred not to know, such as an unexpected half-sibling or a parent who is not, biologically speaking, a parent. And a smaller number may find that the information has consequences they did not foresee, whether in a police investigation, an insurance application or a family dispute.

What, then, might a more responsible approach look like? One possibility is regulatory: clearer rules about how genetic data may be stored, shared and sold, with meaningful penalties for misuse. Another is cultural. We might come to regard the decision to have one's DNA tested less as a private purchase and more as something to be discussed, at least with close relatives, beforehand. This would not be a requirement, still less a veto, but a recognition that the information one is about to release is not entirely one's own.

I am not arguing that nobody should take these tests. The curiosity that drives people to them is understandable, and the pleasure of discovering a forgotten branch of the family is real. I took one myself, some years ago, and had the results explained to me by a genetic counsellor, which I would recommend to anyone considering it. But I did so without thinking of my cousins, and I suspect that is true of most customers. It is that omission, rather than the test itself, that seems to me worth reconsidering.

The language used to market these products speaks of discovery, of finding out who you really are. The more accurate message might be rather less flattering: that who you are is inseparable from who they are, and that what you choose to reveal about yourself, you are also revealing about them.

6.title: The Farm That Let Go
paragraphs: Had you driven past Hollins Farm fifteen years ago, you would have seen what looked like a model of agricultural order: hedges trimmed square, fields of winter wheat running to the horizon, not a thistle out of place. Drive past today and you might assume the owners had died, or emigrated, or simply given up. The hedges have swollen into thickets. Scrub and young oak have crept across the old wheat fields. In the valley bottom, where a straightened stream once ran in a neat ditch, there is now a sprawling, untidy wetland, full of fallen branches and the sound of frogs.

The owners have done none of those things. Ruth and Callum Mercer still live in the farmhouse, and they are, if anything, busier than they were when they farmed conventionally. What they gave up was not the land but the attempt to control it. 'If we hadn't been losing money every year, we probably wouldn't be here now,' Ruth told me, standing at the edge of what used to be their best field. 'People assume we did it for idealistic reasons. The truth is, we were desperate.'

The farm had been running at a loss for most of a decade. The soil, ploughed and fertilised for generations, had grown thin and compacted; yields were falling, and the costs of fuel and chemicals were rising. Were it not for the subsidies they received, the Mercers would have gone bankrupt years earlier. When a conservation charity approached them with a proposal to let the land 'rewild' under supervision, they agreed, as Callum puts it, 'mostly because we couldn't think of anything worse that could happen'.

What happened instead surprised everyone, including the charity. Within three years, the number of bird species recorded on the farm had nearly doubled. Rare butterflies that had not been seen in the county for decades reappeared along the edges of the scrub. Small herds of hardy cattle and pigs, introduced to mimic the grazing and rooting of long-vanished wild animals, began to create a patchwork of open glades and dense cover that turned out to suit a far wider range of creatures than the uniform fields had done.

The most dramatic change came with the beavers. A licensed pair was released into the stream six years ago, and they set about rearranging the valley with an energy that no engineer could have matched. Their dams slowed the water and spread it sideways into the surrounding land, creating the wetland that now dominates the valley floor. The effects have been felt well beyond the farm's boundaries. During a severe storm two winters ago, the village downstream, which had flooded three times in the previous decade, stayed dry. Hydrologists who studied the event concluded that, but for the beaver dams holding back the water, the peak flow through the village would have been significantly higher.

Not everyone has been won over. Neighbouring farmers complain that the scrub harbours foxes and weeds that spread onto their own land. Some local people, attached to the tidy landscape they grew up with, regard the farm as an eyesore and the project as a waste of good agricultural land at a time when food security is a growing concern. 'Supposing every farmer did what they've done,' one neighbour said, 'where would our food come from?'

It is a fair question, and the Mercers do not dismiss it. They point out that their land was among the least productive in the area and that rewilding makes most sense on precisely such marginal ground, where the costs of farming outweigh the returns. They also note that the farm still produces food, in the form of meat from the free-roaming cattle and pigs, albeit in much smaller quantities than before. Their income now comes from a mixture of meat sales, nature tourism, conservation grants and payments for the carbon stored in the regenerating soil and woodland.

Whether that model could be widely replicated is uncertain. Much depends on government policy, which in many countries is shifting towards rewarding farmers for environmental benefits as well as food production. Should those payments be reduced in future, projects like this could become far harder to sustain. Provided they continue, however, ecologists believe that rewilding marginal land could make a substantial contribution to reversing the decline in wildlife, without significantly affecting national food supplies.

Walking back to the farmhouse at dusk, Ruth stopped to point out a barn owl quartering the rough grass where the wheat used to grow. She had not seen one on the farm in twenty years. 'If you'd told me then that I'd end up being proud of all this mess,' she said, 'I'd have laughed at you.' She is not laughing now. Or rather, she is, but for an entirely different reason.

6.title: Not Just Any Tree, Not Just Anywhere
paragraphs: There are few environmental causes as easy to love as tree planting. It is visible, hopeful and pleasingly simple: put a sapling in the ground, wait, and watch it pull carbon out of the sky. Governments announce targets measured in billions of trees; companies promise to plant one for every product sold; schoolchildren are photographed in muddy boots, spades in hand. Were I a politician in search of a popular policy, I would find it hard to think of a better one. And that, I am afraid, is part of the problem.

Let me be clear from the outset. Forests are indispensable. They store vast quantities of carbon, regulate rainfall, stabilise soils and shelter a large share of the world's land-based species. Had we not cleared so many of them over the past two centuries, we would be facing a considerably less severe climate crisis today. Protecting and restoring forests is, beyond any reasonable doubt, one of the most important things humanity can do. My objection is not to trees. It is to the assumption that planting them is straightforwardly good, wherever and however it is done.

Consider, first, the question of where. Not every treeless landscape is a forest waiting to happen. Grasslands, peat bogs and savannahs are ecosystems in their own right, many of them rich in wildlife and, in the case of peat, far more effective at storing carbon than the conifers sometimes planted on top of them. Planting trees on a healthy peat bog, which requires draining it first, can release more carbon than the trees will absorb for decades. Supposing a scheme of that kind were judged by the number of saplings alone, it would look like a triumph. Judged by its effect on the atmosphere, it would be a failure.

Then there is the question of what. A great deal of the planting carried out under ambitious national targets consists of fast-growing monocultures, often of a single non-native species, laid out in rows. Such plantations can be valuable sources of timber, but they support far less wildlife than mixed native woodland, are more vulnerable to disease and fire, and, if harvested on short cycles, may return much of their carbon to the atmosphere within a generation. To count them as equivalent to a restored natural forest is, at best, optimistic accounting.

Finally, there is the question of survival. A sapling is not a tree. Studies of large-scale planting campaigns have found that, in some cases, a majority of the young trees died within a few years, through drought, grazing or simple neglect once the cameras had gone. A target met on the day of planting tells us very little about what will be standing in twenty years. Should funding be tied only to the number planted rather than the number that survive, this outcome is all but guaranteed.

None of this would matter greatly if tree planting were merely one tool among many. The danger is that it has become something else: a substitute for harder decisions. A company that promises to plant a million trees may be less inclined to reduce the emissions that made the trees necessary in the first place. A government that celebrates its planting figures may be quietly approving the clearance of ancient woodland for a new road. Given the choice between protecting an old forest and planting a new one, the old forest is almost always the better bet, since it may take centuries for a plantation to match its carbon stores and biodiversity.

What, then, would a better approach look like? It would start by protecting what already exists. It would favour natural regeneration, letting land recover on its own with the seeds already present in the soil, wherever that is feasible; this is often cheaper and produces more resilient woodland than planting. Where planting is necessary, it would use a mix of native species suited to local conditions, chosen in consultation with the communities who will live alongside them. And it would measure success not in saplings but in hectares of healthy, growing forest a decade or more later.

Unless we make that shift, I fear we will look back on the great planting campaigns of this decade as a missed opportunity, one in which enormous goodwill and considerable money were spent on gestures that photographed well but delivered less than they promised. Otherwise, there is no reason why they should not succeed. The enthusiasm is real, and so is the need.
So by all means plant a tree. But ask, first, whether it is the right tree, in the right place, and whether anyone will be there to look after it once the photographers have gone home.

7.title: Who Needs Critics?
paragraphs: Every few years, someone declares the death of the critic, and every few years the critic declines to die. The latest obituary was prompted by the rise of recommendation algorithms and star ratings, which, we are told, have made the professional reviewer redundant. Why read a twelve-hundred-word essay on a new novel when a few thousand readers have already given it an average of four point two out of five? Why trust one person's taste when you can consult everyone's? The argument is superficially persuasive. I think it is profoundly mistaken, and I want to explain why.

Start with what a rating actually tells you. A score of four point two is a summary of approval, and approval is a perfectly useful thing to know. But it tells you almost nothing about why people approved, or whether the reasons that pleased them would please you. A thriller that is utterly gripping and a quietly devastating literary novel may receive identical scores from entirely different audiences. The number flattens them into equivalence. A good critic does the opposite: she distinguishes, she explains, she tells you what kind of experience a work offers and what it asks of you in return.

The algorithm, for its part, does something subtler and, in a sense, more limiting. It recommends what people like you have liked before. That is very helpful if you want more of the same, and rather less so if you do not. It is designed, quite deliberately, to minimise disappointment, and in doing so it also minimises surprise. Yet some of the most important encounters any of us have with art are with works we would never have chosen: the film we saw because a friend insisted, the strange, slow, difficult book that bored us for fifty pages and then rearranged the way we see the world. A critic who is any good is, among other things, a professional insister.

None of this is to romanticise the profession. Critics can be lazy, cliquish and absurdly pleased with their own cleverness; some write chiefly to be quoted, others chiefly to wound. A great deal of reviewing has always been little more than consumer advice dressed up in elegant prose. And it would be naive to pretend that critical consensus is free of fashion, snobbery or the influence of publishers' marketing budgets. If the algorithm is fallible, so, unquestionably, are we.

But the best criticism has never been primarily about telling people what to buy. It is about attention: the patient, informed, slightly obsessive attention to how a work is made and what it is doing. A first-rate review of a painting might draw your eye to the way a single cold blue shadow organises an entire canvas. A good review of a film might show you why a scene that seemed merely slow was in fact the emotional hinge of the whole story. You may disagree with the critic's verdict, and often you should. Even so, you will see the work more clearly for having argued with her.

That last point is perhaps the crux. Criticism is not a substitute for one's own judgement; it is a provocation to it. A rating invites agreement or indifference, and very little else. A strong, well-argued review invites a response. It gives you something to push against, and in pushing you discover what you actually think. Many readers can name a critic whose opinions they almost invariably disagree with and whom they nonetheless read faithfully, precisely because the disagreement is so productive.

There is also a wider cultural function that ratings cannot perform. Critics, at their best, make arguments about value in public. They ask what a society chooses to celebrate and what it overlooks, whose work gets reviewed and whose does not. They can champion difficult, unfashionable or marginal art that would never accumulate enough ratings to surface in anyone's recommendations. When a once-neglected writer is rediscovered, it is very often because a critic insisted, against the indifference of the market, that she deserved another look.

So is the critic necessary? Not in the sense that anyone needs to be told what to like. But if we want a culture in which art is argued about rather than merely consumed, in which taste is something we develop rather than something that is predicted for us, then yes, I believe so. The algorithm can tell you what you will probably enjoy. Only a critic can tell you why something matters, and occasionally persuade you that it matters even though you did not enjoy it at all.

Perhaps the obituary writers will be proved right eventually. I hope not. And if they are, I suspect we will find ourselves missing, rather sooner than we expect, the sound of someone arguing passionately about a book we have not yet read.

7.title: A Quietly Extraordinary Retrospective
paragraphs: It is a rare exhibition that makes you want to apologise to the artist. Inés Carvallo, who died in 1991 in relative obscurity, spent forty years painting small, unassuming interiors: kitchen tables, half-open doors, an empty chair by a rain-streaked window. During her lifetime, critics who noticed her at all tended to describe her work as charming, pleasant or, most damningly, modest. The current retrospective, the first full survey of her career, makes those adjectives look not merely inadequate but faintly ridiculous. This is a profoundly ambitious body of work that happens to be painted on a small scale. The two are not the same thing, and it has taken us an unconscionably long time to notice the difference.

The exhibition is arranged chronologically, which in this case is exactly the right decision. The early rooms show a competent, somewhat derivative young painter working through the influences of her training: there are echoes of the Dutch masters in the handling of light, and rather too obvious borrowings from the French intimists in the colour. These are perfectly decent pictures. Few of them, though, would have persuaded you that their author would become one of the most original painters of her generation, and I suspect the curators know it. They have wisely kept this section brief.

Then something changes. Around 1962, after the death of her husband, Carvallo stopped painting people altogether. The interiors empty out. What remains are rooms in which someone has evidently just been present, or is about to arrive: a cup with a spoon still in it, a coat thrown over the back of a chair, a book face down at a page the reader never returned to. It would be easy to read these as straightforwardly elegiac, and some undoubtedly are. But the finest of them are stranger than that. They seem less concerned with absence than with attention itself, with the peculiar quality of a room when no one is looking at it.

Technically, the mature work is quite remarkable. Carvallo built up her surfaces in thin, translucent layers, sometimes dozens of them, so that the colours seem to glow from within rather than sit on the surface. A whitewashed wall in one painting from the late sixties turns out, on close inspection, to contain pale greens, warm ochres and a barely perceptible violet. Step back, and it is simply white, though a white so alive that it makes the real walls of the gallery look dead by comparison. I have rarely seen paint used with such patient, almost stubborn, precision.

The centrepiece of the show, and the work most visitors will remember, is a slightly larger canvas from 1974, showing a narrow, sun-filled corridor ending in a closed door. Nothing happens in it. There is no figure, no object of obvious significance, merely light falling across bare floorboards. And yet it is absolutely gripping. I stood in front of it for a long time, and so, I noticed, did nearly everyone else. Quite why it should be so affecting is hard to say. Perhaps it is the sense that the door might open at any moment; perhaps it is the sense that it never will.

If the exhibition has a weakness, it lies in the final room, devoted to the work of her last decade. Failing eyesight forced Carvallo to work more broadly, and the late paintings, while undeniably moving as documents of a struggle, lack the extraordinary control of the middle years. The curators present them with what feels like slightly excessive reverence. A more selective hang would have served her better, and would have allowed the show to end on a high note rather than a fairly muted one.

That reservation aside, this is an utterly absorbing exhibition and, in its quiet way, a deeply important one. It raises uncomfortable questions about why Carvallo was overlooked for so long. Her subject matter, domestic, interior and small-scale, was for decades associated with women painters and therefore treated, almost automatically, as minor. Her refusal to promote herself did not help, nor did her decision to remain in a provincial city far from the major galleries. None of this tells us anything about the quality of her work. All of it tells us a good deal about the habits of the art world.

Go, and give yourself time. These are not paintings that reveal themselves at a glance; they reward the kind of slow, sustained looking that most of us rarely give to anything. Do so, and you may find, as I did, that you leave the gallery seeing ordinary rooms a little differently, and wondering how many other quietly extraordinary artists we have managed to miss.

8.title: The Art of Not Quite Saying
paragraphs: When a large company announced last spring that it was 'rightsizing its workforce to unlock future growth', several thousand people learned, in effect, that they had lost their jobs. Nobody in the announcement was dismissed, sacked or made redundant. Positions were 'impacted'. Colleagues were 'transitioned'. The chief executive spoke warmly of a 'difficult but necessary journey'. One former employee, interviewed by a local radio station, put it more simply. 'I wish they had just told us the truth,' she said. 'It's as if they thought we wouldn't notice we'd been fired.'

Euphemism is as old as language. Every culture has its polite ways of referring to death, illness, bodily functions and other matters that make people uncomfortable, and many of these serve an entirely humane purpose. To say that someone has 'passed away' rather than 'died' is not, in most contexts, an attempt to deceive. It is a way of softening a blow, of signalling sympathy, of acknowledging that some facts are painful to hear stated baldly. Much as we may mock such phrases, few of us would wish to do without them at a funeral.

The language of the corporate announcement belongs to a different category. Its purpose is not to spare the feelings of the listener but to protect the speaker from the consequences of what is being said. The writer George Orwell, who devoted a famous essay to the subject, argued that political language of this kind is designed 'to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable'. That may sound excessive when applied to a press release about restructuring. The mechanism, however, is the same: an action with a clear agent and clear victims is reframed as an impersonal process, something that simply happened, like the weather.

Consider how often the passive voice and abstract nouns appear in such statements. 'Mistakes were made' is the classic example, a sentence that admits an error while carefully declining to say who made it. Military briefings speak of 'collateral damage' rather than civilians killed; prison systems refer to 'enhanced interrogation' rather than torture; governments announce 'fiscal consolidation' rather than cuts to schools and hospitals. In each case the vocabulary performs a kind of moral anaesthesia. The listener understands, at some level, what is being described, but the words have been chosen so that nothing quite registers.

Critics of this tendency are sometimes accused of pedantry. Language changes, the argument goes, and insisting that every term be blunt would make public life impossibly harsh. There is something to this. Diplomacy, for example, depends on a degree of studied vagueness, and a negotiator who said exactly what he thought at every stage would rarely reach agreement. Notwithstanding these exceptions, though, the line between tact and evasion is usually easier to draw than defenders of doublespeak suggest. The test is simple: does the phrase help the listener understand, or does it help the speaker avoid responsibility?

The cost of failing that test is not merely aesthetic. When official language consistently obscures who did what to whom, citizens lose the ability to hold anyone accountable. It is difficult to protest against a 'workforce optimisation'; it is considerably easier to protest against the dismissal of three thousand workers. This is why campaigners have long insisted that the first step in any struggle for justice is to name the problem plainly. Many of the most effective movements of the last century began, in a sense, as campaigns of translation, replacing an official euphemism with a word that made people angry.

Some institutions have begun to respond. A number of public bodies now require that official communications be written in plain language, and several have published guidelines discouraging terms that conceal the agent of an action. The results are uneven, and the guidelines themselves are not always followed. But the principle seems sound. However uncomfortable plain speech may be for those in power, it is a precondition of democratic scrutiny.

It is high time, perhaps, that the rest of us adopted a similar discipline. Euphemism is not only something done to us by press offices; it is something we do ourselves, at work and at home, whenever we would rather not take responsibility for an unpleasant decision. We 'let people go', we 'pursue other opportunities', we suggest that a relationship 'didn't work out', as though it had failed of its own accord. Some of these softenings are kind. Others are merely convenient, albeit in ways we may not care to examine.

The former employee who spoke to the radio station had a final remark. She said she would rather have been told 'You're fired' to her face than read about 'workforce transition' in an email. 'At least then,' she said, 'I'd have known someone was actually responsible.' It is a fair summary of what is at stake. Plain language does not make bad news any better. It does, however, make it possible to argue back.

8.title: Ordinary People, Hard Questions
paragraphs: Imagine being chosen, more or less at random, to help decide a question your government has been avoiding for twenty years. A letter arrives. You are invited, along with ninety-nine other residents selected by lottery to reflect the population in age, gender, region and background, to spend six weekends hearing evidence, questioning experts and debating with strangers. At the end, you will vote on recommendations that will be submitted to parliament. You are paid for your time. You may say no, but most people, it turns out, say yes.

This is the citizens' assembly, and over the past two decades it has moved from the margins of political theory into the practice of a growing number of democracies. Assemblies have deliberated on electoral reform, climate policy, end-of-life care and some of the most divisive moral questions societies face. Their supporters regard them as a cure for much that ails representative politics: polarisation, short-termism and the suspicion that decisions are made by a professional class remote from ordinary life. Their detractors regard them, at best, as expensive theatre.

I should declare an interest. Some years ago I attended an assembly as an observer, and I came away more impressed than I had expected to be. The participants included a retired lorry driver, a pharmacist, a student who had never voted and a farmer who announced on the first morning that he had come 'to make sure nobody did anything daft'. By the final weekend, he was among the most thoughtful contributors in the room. What struck me most was not that people changed their minds, although some did, but how seriously they took the obligation to understand views they did not share.

Much of this, I think, has to do with the conditions. Politicians argue in public, under the eyes of journalists and party whips, with every concession liable to be reported as a defeat. Assembly members deliberate in small groups, guided by trained facilitators, with time to ask naive questions and no career to protect. It is hardly surprising that they behave differently. If only parliaments could reproduce those conditions, many of their pathologies might ease. They cannot, of course, which is precisely the argument for assemblies as a complement to them.

The objections deserve a hearing. The first is that assemblies lack democratic legitimacy: nobody elected the members, and they cannot be voted out. This is true, albeit a little odd as a criticism, since the whole point of random selection is to produce a body that looks more like the population than any elected chamber does. A second objection is more serious. Assemblies depend heavily on the experts who brief them and the organisers who set their agenda, and a poorly designed process could steer participants towards conclusions chosen in advance. Safeguards exist, such as balanced panels of witnesses and independent oversight, but they are only as good as the people who enforce them.

The third objection, and the one I find hardest to dismiss, concerns what happens afterwards. An assembly that produces careful recommendations which the government then ignores may do more harm than good, confirming the cynicism it was meant to dispel. There have been cases where this has happened, and the participants' sense of betrayal was palpable. It is essential, therefore, that any government convening an assembly commit in advance to responding formally to each recommendation, explaining publicly which it accepts and why it rejects the others.

Notwithstanding these difficulties, the record so far is encouraging. Where assemblies have been taken seriously, they have helped break deadlocks on questions that elected politicians found too dangerous to touch. Their recommendations have often been more ambitious than politicians expected, and more nuanced than either side of a polarised debate would have predicted. Perhaps most importantly, participants almost invariably report a greater trust in democratic institutions, and in their fellow citizens, than they had before.

I would not suggest that assemblies replace elections, still less that every decision be delegated to randomly chosen citizens. Representative democracy, for all its faults, remains the best mechanism yet devised for holding power to account. But it is high time we stopped treating ordinary people as a problem to be managed and started treating them as a resource. The farmer who came to make sure nobody did anything daft put it rather well on the last day. 'I'd rather they asked people like us more often,' he said. 'We don't always get it right. But at least we're not pretending to know everything.'
Far be it from me to improve on that.
