9.title: The Summit We Were Not to Reach
paragraphs: We left the hut at three in the morning, under a sky so crowded with stars that it seemed almost vulgar. There were four of us: Marta, who had organised the trip and was to lead the final section; her brother Joaquín, by far the most experienced of us; a quiet Austrian engineer called Lukas; and me, the least experienced, who had been training for this for a year and was determined not to be the reason we turned back. We were about to attempt a peak that none of us had climbed before, by a route that, according to the guidebook, was 'serious but straightforward in good conditions'. It was the last four words that would come to matter.

For the first three hours, everything went as planned. The snow was firm, the wind light, the ridge exactly as the photographs had promised. I remember thinking, with the dangerous euphoria of the well-prepared amateur, that this was going to be easier than I had feared. In retrospect, that thought should have worried me more than it did. Experienced climbers have a saying that the mountain does not know how much you have trained, and I was soon to discover what it meant.

Around dawn, the weather began to turn. It did not happen dramatically. A thin veil of cloud drifted across the summit, then another; the wind picked up, though not by much; the temperature, if anything, rose slightly. None of these signs was alarming in itself. Taken together, however, they amounted to something Joaquín did not like, and he said so. Marta, who had been watching the same sky, agreed that the forecast had probably been optimistic, but she pointed out, reasonably enough, that we were only two hours from the top and that conditions might improve as the morning went on.

What followed was the most instructive conversation I have ever witnessed, conducted at four thousand metres in a rising wind. Nobody raised their voice. Joaquín set out the case for turning back: the cloud was thickening, the descent would take longer than the ascent, and an afternoon storm, if it came, would catch us on the most exposed part of the ridge. Marta set out the case for continuing: the forecast had not mentioned storms, we were strong, and we might never have another chance. Lukas, characteristically, asked a series of precise questions about timing. I said nothing, partly out of deference and partly because I badly wanted to go on and did not trust myself to admit it.

Researchers who study decision-making in the mountains have identified a set of traps into which even skilled climbers reliably fall. One is familiarity: the more often we have done something safely, the less attention we pay to its risks. Another is what has been called summit fever, the tendency for the desire to reach a goal to intensify as it draws nearer, precisely when the cost of pursuing it is often greatest. A third is the reluctance of individuals within a group to voice doubts, particularly if they are less experienced or less confident than the others. I was, that morning, a textbook example of the third.

In the end, it was Marta who made the decision, and she made it against her own inclination. We would give it thirty more minutes, she said, and if the summit was still in cloud, we would turn round, no further discussion. Thirty minutes later the summit had vanished entirely. She looked at it for a long moment, then nodded, and we began the descent. I felt a disappointment so intense that it was almost physical. I also felt, underneath it, an enormous relief, which I would not have admitted to anyone at the time.

The storm arrived at two o'clock that afternoon, by which point we were back at the hut, drinking tea and pretending not to watch the window. A party of three who had been climbing the same ridge on the other side, and who had decided to push on, was forced to spend the night in an emergency shelter. They survived, though one of them lost two toes to frostbite. When we met them the following day, they were cheerful and slightly embarrassed, and nobody said what everyone was thinking.

I have thought about that morning many times since, and about the difference between courage and stubbornness, which is so often invisible until afterwards. It would be comforting to believe that we turned back because we were wise. The truth is more complicated. We turned back because one person spoke up, another listened, and a third was willing to set a clear rule and keep to it. Had any of those things failed to happen, I suspect we would have carried on, and the story I am telling would be very different, if I were telling it at all.

We never did climb that peak. Marta went back the following year with Joaquín and reached the summit in perfect weather. She sent me a photograph from the top, with a single line of text: 'Serious but straightforward in good conditions.' I keep it above my desk, as a reminder that the conditions are the part we do not control, and that knowing when to turn round is not a failure of ambition but its most difficult form.

9.title: The Hardest Training Is Rest
paragraphs: When the distance runner Amara Okoye withdrew from a major championship two seasons ago, the announcement ran to three sentences and gave no reason beyond 'personal health'. Within hours, social media had supplied several. She was injured; she was out of form; she had fallen out with her coach; she was, in the phrase one commentator chose, 'not mentally tough enough for the big stage'. The last of these, Okoye later said, was the one that stung, not least because it was so nearly the opposite of the truth.

What had actually happened was that, after six years of competing at the highest level, she had stopped sleeping. She would lie awake running through race plans, split times and worst-case scenarios, then train twice the next day on three or four hours of rest. Her times were, if anything, improving. It was her physiotherapist who first noticed that something was wrong, prompted by an apparently trivial detail: Okoye, who had always been meticulous, had begun to forget appointments. Within a month she had been diagnosed with severe burnout, and her medical team advised her to stop competing altogether for at least six months.

Okoye's case is far from unique. Over the past decade, a growing number of elite athletes have spoken publicly about anxiety, depression and exhaustion, and in doing so have begun to shift a culture that for generations treated psychological difficulty as a private weakness to be overcome rather than a health problem to be treated. Sports psychologists have welcomed the change, while cautioning against a narrative in which every disclosure is framed as heroic. The point, as one put it to me, is not that athletes who struggle are especially brave; it is that struggling is ordinary, and that the conditions of elite sport make it more likely.

Those conditions are well documented. Elite athletes typically train for many hours a day, often from early adolescence, in environments where performance is measured with extraordinary precision and failure is public. Their identities, and frequently their incomes, are bound up with results over which they have only partial control. Injury can end a career overnight. Moreover, the qualities that make them successful, such as perfectionism, a willingness to tolerate pain and an ability to ignore discomfort, may also make them slow to recognise when they need help.

It follows that the most significant changes are likely to be structural rather than individual. Some national federations now require that psychological support be made available to all funded athletes, not merely to those in crisis. Others have introduced routine screening for sleep problems and signs of overtraining, on the grounds that physical and mental fatigue are closely intertwined. A small number of coaches have begun to build mandatory rest periods into training plans, treating recovery not as time lost but as part of the work. Whether such measures will prove effective in the long run remains to be seen, but early indications are promising.

There is, nevertheless, a tension that no policy can entirely resolve. Elite sport is, by its nature, about pushing the body and mind towards their limits, and athletes who refuse to take risks rarely win. The question, then, is not how to remove risk altogether, which would be neither possible nor desirable, but how to distinguish between a calculated risk and a reckless one. Training through mild discomfort before an important race may be entirely sensible. Training through months of insomnia, as Okoye did, is something else. The difficulty is that from the inside, as she herself has acknowledged, the two can feel remarkably similar.

Okoye's own recovery was neither quick nor linear. For the first few weeks, she said, she felt guilty every morning she did not run, as though she were betraying the people who had invested in her. She was on the point of returning to training several times, and each time her team persuaded her to wait. What eventually helped, alongside therapy, was a series of conversations with retired athletes, several of whom told her that they wished they had stopped sooner. 'They weren't telling me to give up,' she said. 'They were telling me that taking a break wasn't the same thing.'

She returned to competition fourteen months after her withdrawal. Her first race back was, by her own standards, unremarkable; she finished sixth and was, she said, delighted. She has since set a personal best, and she speaks about her burnout with a frankness that would have been almost unthinkable for an athlete of her standing a generation ago. Asked whether she worries that her openness might be held against her, she shrugged. 'People were going to talk anyway,' she said. 'At least now they're talking about something real.'

Perhaps the most telling detail of her story concerns the physiotherapist who first noticed the missed appointments. Had she dismissed them, as she might easily have done, Okoye believes she would have carried on until something broke. Her advice to younger athletes is accordingly simple: surround yourself with people who will notice, and learn to listen when they speak up. In a culture that still celebrates the ability to push through, that may be the hardest training of all.

10.title: A Library for Readers Not Yet Born
paragraphs: In a forest outside a northern European city, a thousand spruce trees are growing in neat rows. By the time they are ready to be felled, in about eighty years, most of the people who planted them will be dead. The trees are destined to become paper, and the paper is to be used to print an anthology of a hundred books, one contributed each year by a different writer. None of the manuscripts will be read until then. They are kept, sealed, in a wood-lined room in the city's public library, where visitors can see the titles but not a single word of the texts.

The project, which by the time it concludes will have been running for a century, was conceived as an experiment in what its founder calls 'cathedral thinking': the willingness to begin something whose completion you will not live to see. The writers who contribute know that they will never hear how their work is received. Several have said that this is precisely its appeal. Free of reviews, sales figures and the pressure to be topical, they are writing, as one of them put it, 'for people we can only imagine, about a world we cannot predict'.

It is easy to be charmed by such schemes and equally easy to be cynical about them. Critics have pointed out that a library of sealed manuscripts is every bit as vulnerable to fire, flood or political upheaval as any other building, and that the readers of the future may be nowhere near as interested in our books as we would like them to be. Both points are fair. Yet the project's value lies less in the certainty of its outcome than in the habit of mind it tries to cultivate. We live, as many observers have noted, in an age of extraordinary short-termism. Companies report their profits quarterly; politicians plan for the next election; news is measured in minutes. Against that background, a commitment measured in generations is not merely unusual. It is almost subversive.

Long-term thinking of this kind was once far more common. Medieval masons laid foundations for cathedrals that would take centuries to complete. Farmers planted oaks for their grandchildren's ships. The proverb that society grows great when old people plant trees in whose shade they will never sit is older than any of the institutions now trying to revive it. What seems to have changed is not our capacity to think ahead but the incentives that reward us for doing so. The further into the future a benefit lies, the less it appears to be worth to us now, a tendency economists call discounting and the rest of us might simply call impatience.

The consequences are most obvious in relation to the environment. Decisions taken in this decade about energy, land and water will shape the conditions in which people are living well into the next century. By 2100, a child born today will have been living with the effects of those decisions for her entire life. Yet the people most affected have no vote, no voice and no lobbyists. Some countries have experimented with ways of representing them: one has appointed a commissioner for future generations, whose task is to assess whether public bodies are taking long-term consequences into account. Another is due to introduce a requirement that major legislation be accompanied by an assessment of its effects fifty years ahead. Whether such measures will make much difference is uncertain, but they are, at the very least, an acknowledgement of the problem.

There is, of course, a risk of grandiosity in all this. Nobody can know what the people of 2100 will value, and it would be presumptuous to plan their lives for them. The most thoughtful advocates of long-term thinking are careful to distinguish between imposing our preferences on the future and preserving its options. Planting a forest, protecting a language or keeping a library open does not dictate what future generations will do; it simply ensures that they have more to choose from. As the old saying has it, we do not inherit the earth from our ancestors so much as borrow it from our children.

The writers contributing to the forest library seem to understand this instinctively. Their manuscripts, according to those few who have spoken about them, are not prophecies or warnings but simply stories, written in the hope that someone, someday, will find them worth reading. One contributor described handing over her manuscript as 'the most hopeful thing I have ever done', precisely because it assumed that there would be a future, and that it would contain readers.

The spruce trees, meanwhile, are growing. They are on the verge of their first thinning, a routine operation that will remove the weakest so that the rest can thrive. The foresters responsible for them will retire long before the trees are harvested, and will hand them on to successors they have not yet met. It is a small thing, a few hectares of forest and a room full of sealed paper. But it is a reminder that some of the most worthwhile things we do are those whose results we will never see, and that a legacy, in the end, is less about being remembered than about leaving something behind that others can use.

10.title: The Uses of Nostalgia
paragraphs: For most of its history, nostalgia was a disease. The word was coined in the late seventeenth century by a Swiss medical student to describe a condition afflicting soldiers serving far from home: a melancholy so severe that it was thought capable of killing them. Physicians blamed it variously on the change of air, the ringing of cowbells and, in one memorable theory, damage to the eardrums caused by the clanging of Alpine life. Treatments ranged from leeches to threats. It was not until well into the twentieth century that nostalgia shed its medical associations and became what it is today: a mild, bittersweet, slightly embarrassing pleasure.

That embarrassment is worth examining. Nostalgia has a poor reputation among intellectuals, who tend to regard it as sentimental at best and politically dangerous at worst. There is good reason for the suspicion. Longing for a lost golden age is the stock in trade of demagogues, and the past it invokes is almost always a fiction, a time when everyone knew their place and nobody locked their doors, or so we are told. As the saying goes, the good old days were rarely as good as they are remembered, and for many people, they were not good at all.

And yet recent research in psychology suggests that this picture is incomplete. Studies in which participants are asked to recall a nostalgic memory have found, fairly consistently, that the experience tends to raise rather than lower their mood. People who have just been nostalgic report feeling more connected to others, more confident that their lives have meaning, and more optimistic about the future. Far from being a retreat from the present, nostalgia appears in many cases to function as a resource for coping with it, particularly at moments of loneliness, transition or uncertainty.

How can both views be right? Part of the answer lies in a distinction that some scholars have drawn between two kinds of nostalgia. The first, which we might call restorative, seeks to rebuild the lost home exactly as it was, and treats any change as betrayal. This is the nostalgia of political movements that promise to make the nation what it once was. The second, which we might call reflective, dwells on the longing itself, aware that the past cannot be recovered and that memory is partial. It is every bit as emotional as the first, but it is ironic, questioning and, crucially, compatible with change.

Most of the nostalgia that people experience in daily life seems to be of the second kind. The middle-aged man who listens to the music of his adolescence does not, for the most part, wish to return to being sixteen, with all its humiliations. He is revisiting a version of himself that still lives inside him, checking, perhaps, that the thread connecting then to now is intact. In this sense, nostalgia is less about the past than about continuity, a way of reassuring ourselves that we remain recognisably the same people despite everything that has changed around us.

This may explain why nostalgia tends to increase during periods of rapid change. When the familiar landmarks of life are disappearing, whether through ageing, migration, technological upheaval or the loss of people we love, the need for continuity becomes more acute. It is no coincidence that interest in old photographs, recipes and family histories often surges during difficult years. People are not hiding from the future; they are gathering what they need to face it.

None of this rehabilitates the restorative variety. The politics of the lost golden age remains as misleading as ever, and the more vividly it is described, the more suspicious we should be. But a blanket dismissal of nostalgia risks throwing the baby out with the bathwater. To feel affection for what has gone is not the same as wanting it back, and to treat every expression of longing as reactionary is to misunderstand one of the most ordinary ways in which human beings make sense of time.

There is, I think, a further point. A society that has no use for nostalgia may find it harder to value what it has. Our sense of what is worth preserving, a building, a dialect, a tradition, often begins with the recognition that it might one day be lost, and with the anticipatory nostalgia that recognition produces. By the time a neighbourhood has been demolished, it is too late to campaign for it. Those who feel a pang of loss in advance are sometimes the only ones who act in time.

So I have stopped apologising for my own nostalgia, which mostly takes the form of an unreasonable attachment to the radio programmes of my childhood. I do not believe they were better than what is broadcast today; in many respects, they were nowhere near as good. But listening to them reminds me of the kitchen where I first heard them, and of the people who were there, and that is reason enough. The past, as a much-quoted line has it, is a foreign country. It does no harm to visit, as long as we remember to come home.
